title: The Tafsir Tradition
bigQuestion: How did classical Muslim scholars decide what a verse of the Qur'an means, and why did they so often disagree?

story.title: Four Shelves, One Verse
story.kicker: Four scholars, four centuries, one verse about light, and four different first sentences.
paragraphs: Picture a reading room in a large library. On the table sit four thick commentaries on the Qur'an, each open to the same verse: Surah al-Nur (24), ayah 35, the Light Verse. It says that God is the light of the heavens and the earth, and it compares that light to a lamp in a niche, in a glass, lit from a blessed olive tree. The four books were written in four different centuries, in Baghdad, in Khwarazm, in Herat and in Damascus. Each author read the same Arabic words. Each began his explanation differently.

The oldest book is by al-Tabari, who died in 923. His first move is to gather reports. He lists what early Muslims said the verse meant, name by name, chain by chain. One report says the light is God's guidance for the people of the heavens and the earth. Another says the lamp stands for the light of faith in a believer's heart. Only after the reports does al-Tabari say which reading he prefers.

The second book, al-Zamakhshari's Kashshaf from the twelfth century, opens with grammar and rhetoric. What kind of sentence is this? Is it a metaphor? What does the word for niche mean, and why does the verse pile image on image? For him the verse is a parable, and the job of the commentator is to show how the figure of speech works.

The third book, by Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, who died in 1210, asks what light itself is. He brings in philosophy, physics as his age understood it, and theology. Can God be called light in a literal sense? He lists opinions, argues against some and defends one. The fourth book, by Ibn Kathir of Damascus, who died in 1373, turns back to reports and hadith. He explains the verse first by other verses, then by what Muhammad's Companions said, in the manner of his teacher Ibn Taymiyya.

Four scholars, four methods. All of them were Muslims who believed the words were God's. All of them wrote in Arabic and used the same grammar books. Yet the first sentence of each explanation shows a different idea of what explaining even means. This chapter is about those methods: what they were, who used them, and what tools they shared.
story.think: If four expert readers of one text begin from four different questions, does that show the text is unclear, or does it show something about reading itself? Explain your view.

lessons.title: The Word Tafsir
lessons.mainIdea: Tafsir is the Muslim discipline of explaining the Qur'an verse by verse, and it began, Muslims say, with the Prophet and his Companions.
reading: *Tafsir* is an Arabic word that means explanation or unveiling. In Islamic scholarship it names a whole discipline: the study of what each verse of the Qur'an means, word by word and verse by verse. A scholar who writes such a work is a *mufassir*. A commentary is also called a tafsir, so the word names both the activity and the book. The great classical commentaries run to many volumes, because they explain all 114 surahs in order, from al-Fatiha (1) to al-Nas (114).

Muslims trace the discipline to Muhammad himself. Surah al-Nahl (16), ayah 44, says the Qur'an was sent down to the Prophet so that he might make clear to people what was sent down to them. Muslim scholars read this as the first charter of tafsir: the Prophet explained the text, and his *Companions* passed on what he said. One Companion, Ibn Abbas (d. c. 687), became known in tradition as the interpreter of the Qur'an, and later commentaries quote him constantly.

A second word matters here. *Ta'wil* also means interpretation, but in later usage it often points to a deeper or figurative sense, beyond the plain wording. Some scholars used tafsir and ta'wil as synonyms. Others, especially Sufi and Shia writers, kept ta'wil for inner meanings. Al-Tabari, as we will see, called his own book an explanation of the ta'wil of the Qur'an, so the two words were not fixed in the early period.

Why does a text need explanation at all? Scholars gave several reasons. The Qur'an uses rare Arabic words. It refers to events without naming them. It gives commands whose scope is unclear. It uses images and parables. And its readers, within a century, included many people whose first language was not Arabic. Tafsir grew to answer these needs, and by the tenth century it had become one of the central sciences of Islam.

words.d: explanation of the Qur'an, verse by verse; also the name for a commentary that does this
a scholar who writes a tafsir; the plural is mufassirun
interpretation; in later usage, often a deeper or figurative reading beyond the plain sense
the men and women who knew Muhammad personally; in Muslim tradition, the first source of tafsir after the Prophet

look.title: The Prophet as Explainer
look.text: In Surah al-Nahl (16), ayah 44, the Qur'an says that God sent down the Reminder to the Prophet so that he could make clear to people what had been sent down to them, and so that they might reflect.
look.cite: Qur'an 16:44, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Muslim scholars read this verse as the origin of tafsir. What two tasks does the verse assign, and who is expected to do each?

check.q: What does the word tafsir mean in Islamic scholarship?
choices: The rules for reciting the Qur'an aloud
The explanation of the Qur'an verse by verse, and a book that does this
The chain of memorizers who preserved the text
The Arabic script used to copy the Qur'an
check.why: Tafsir means explanation; it names both the discipline and the commentary. Recitation rules are tajwid, and the script is a separate subject.

check.q: Which Companion did later tradition call the interpreter of the Qur'an?
choices: Ibn Abbas
Ibn Kathir
Abu Bakr
Ibn Arabi
check.why: Ibn Abbas (d. c. 687) was a Companion known in tradition as the interpreter of the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Arabi lived centuries later.

check.q: Which verse do Muslim scholars often cite as the charter for the Prophet's role in explaining the text?
choices: 2:255, the Throne Verse
24:35, the Light Verse
112:1, the surah of sincerity
16:44, on making clear what was sent down
check.why: Surah al-Nahl 16:44 says the Reminder was sent so the Prophet could make clear to people what was sent to them; scholars read this as the basis of tafsir.

lessons.title: Tradition and Reasoned Opinion
lessons.mainIdea: Classical scholars sorted commentary into two kinds, tafsir by transmitted report and tafsir by reasoned opinion, and argued about how far opinion could go.
reading: Suppose you want to know what a rare word in the Qur'an means. You could look for a report from the Prophet or a Companion who explained it. Or you could reason it out from Arabic poetry, grammar and the rest of the Qur'an. Classical scholars gave these two roads names. Commentary built from reports is *tafsir bi'l-ma'thur*, explanation by what has been transmitted. Commentary built from the scholar's own reasoning is *tafsir bi'l-ra'y*, explanation by opinion.

The first road was the safer one in most scholars' eyes. A widely quoted *hadith*, a report of the Prophet's words, warns that whoever speaks about the Qur'an from his own opinion should prepare his seat in the Fire. Many commentators quoted that warning in their introductions. Yet almost no one thought reports alone were enough, because reports contradict each other, cover only some verses, and need sorting by the strength of their chains of transmitters.

So the argument was really about limits. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir leaned on reports but weighed them and chose. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi reasoned freely from grammar, theology and philosophy, but still cited reports. Later writers distinguished praiseworthy opinion, grounded in Arabic and in the sciences of the text, from blameworthy opinion, which followed a scholar's whim or his party's doctrine. Every side accused the others of the second kind.

One early complete commentary shows the stakes. Muqatil ibn Sulayman (d. 767) wrote a tafsir that filled in names, places and details the Qur'an leaves out, often from stories that circulated among Jews and Christians, the so-called *isra'iliyyat*. Later scholars valued his book and also criticized it, because his reports often had no chain at all. Deciding what counts as a trustworthy source was, from the start, the central question of the discipline.

words.d: commentary built from transmitted reports of the Prophet, Companions and early scholars
commentary built from the scholar's own reasoning in language, theology or law
a report of something Muhammad said, did or approved, passed down with a chain of transmitters
stories from Jewish and Christian sources used by some early commentators to fill in details the Qur'an leaves out

look.title: A Report or a Reason?
look.text: A student asks what the word for a certain bird in Surah al-Naml (27) means. Scholar A finds a report from a Companion who named the bird. Scholar B finds the same word in pre-Islamic Arabic poetry and reasons from its use there. The two answers agree. A third scholar has only his own guess. Classical writers would rank these three sources very differently.
look.prompt: Rank the three answers as a classical commentator might, and explain why the hadith warning about opinion applies to one of them but not to the others.

check.q: What is tafsir bi'l-ma'thur?
choices: Commentary written in Persian rather than Arabic
Commentary built from transmitted reports of the Prophet and early Muslims
Commentary on the inner, hidden meanings of the text
Commentary that uses philosophy and natural science
check.why: Ma'thur means transmitted; this kind of tafsir rests on reports. Inner meanings and philosophy belong to other approaches.

check.q: Why did classical scholars not simply rely on reports alone?
choices: Reports were forbidden by the Qur'an
Reports were only written in Greek
Reports contradict one another and cover only some verses
Reports were kept secret by the caliphs
check.why: Even report-based commentators weighed and chose, because reports conflict, cover only some verses, and vary in the strength of their chains.

check.q: Why did later scholars criticize the commentary of Muqatil ibn Sulayman?
choices: He wrote in a language no one could read
He refused to explain any verse at all
He denied that the Qur'an was in Arabic
His stories often came without any chain of transmission
check.why: Muqatil filled in details, often from isra'iliyyat, but many of his reports had no chain, which later scholars saw as a serious weakness.

lessons.title: The Commentator's Toolbox
lessons.mainIdea: Classical commentators shared a set of tools: Arabic grammar, the occasions of revelation, the doctrine of abrogation, and the distinction between clear and ambiguous verses.
reading: Whatever their school, classical commentators reached for the same tools. The first was Arabic itself: grammar, vocabulary and rhetoric. A commentator asked how a word was used in old poetry, which case ending a noun carried, and whether a phrase was a plain statement or a figure of speech. Al-Suyuti (d. 1505), who wrote a famous handbook of the Qur'anic sciences called al-Itqan, listed dozens of such topics that a qualified commentator had to know.

The second tool was history. Many verses respond to a particular event: a question someone asked, a battle, a dispute in Medina. The reports that describe such events are called *asbab al-nuzul*, the occasions of revelation, and al-Wahidi (d. 1075) collected them in a book of that name. Knowing the occasion could settle what a verse was about. It could also raise a new question: does a verse revealed for one occasion apply only to it, or to every similar case? Most scholars answered that the general wording counts, not the particular occasion.

The third tool was *naskh*, abrogation. Scholars held that some later verses replaced the ruling of earlier ones, as the wine verses moved from caution to prohibition. Which verses abrogated which was hotly debated, and lists ranged from a handful to hundreds. The fourth tool came from the Qur'an itself. Surah Al Imran (3), ayah 7, says that some verses are *muhkam*, clear and decisive, while others are *mutashabih*, ambiguous or open to more than one reading. It adds that those with unsteady hearts chase the ambiguous ones.

That verse became a rule for reading. Interpret the unclear in light of the clear. But where does the sentence end? Read one way, 3:7 says only God knows the meaning of the ambiguous verses. Read with a different pause, it says God and those firmly grounded in knowledge know it. Both readings are grammatically possible in the unpointed Arabic, and commentators divided over them. The toolbox, in other words, did not remove disagreement. It gave scholars a shared way to argue.

words.d: the occasions of revelation: reports about the events or questions a verse answered
abrogation: the view that a later verse can replace the ruling of an earlier one
a clear, decisive verse whose meaning scholars treat as settled
an ambiguous verse, open to more than one reading, which 3:7 says should be read in light of the clear ones

look.title: Clear Verses and Ambiguous Ones
look.text: Surah Al Imran (3), ayah 7, says that God sent down the Book with some verses that are clear and form its foundation, and others that are ambiguous. Those with a sickness in their hearts follow the ambiguous ones, seeking discord and seeking their interpretation. Then it says that none knows their interpretation except God, and that those firmly grounded in knowledge say they believe in it all.
look.cite: Qur'an 3:7, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Depending on where a reader pauses, the verse says either that only God knows the interpretation, or that God and the firmly grounded know it. Which reading gives scholars more room, and why would that matter to a commentator?

check.q: What are the asbab al-nuzul?
choices: Reports about the events or questions a verse responded to
The seven approved ways of reciting the Qur'an
The rules of Arabic case endings
The list of verses that replace earlier rulings
check.why: Asbab al-nuzul means occasions of revelation, the reports collected by al-Wahidi and others about a verse's setting. Abrogation is naskh; recitation is a different science.

check.q: According to 3:7 as most commentators read it, how should ambiguous verses be handled?
choices: They should be removed from the text
They should be read in light of the clear verses
They should be recited but never explained
They should be read only by the caliph
check.why: Surah Al Imran 3:7 contrasts muhkam and mutashabih verses; scholars drew the rule that the unclear is interpreted through the clear.

check.q: What did classical scholars mean by naskh?
choices: The art of beautiful Arabic handwriting
The memorization of the whole Qur'an
A later verse replacing the ruling of an earlier one
A prayer said before opening the book
check.why: Naskh is abrogation, the view that a later revelation can supersede an earlier ruling, as in the sequence of wine verses. Scholars disagreed about how many cases there were.

lessons.title: Al-Tabari Gathers the Reports
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Tabari's commentary set the model for report-based tafsir: collect every transmitted reading, then weigh them and state a reasoned choice.
reading: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari was born around 839 in Tabaristan, on the southern shore of the Caspian Sea, and died in Baghdad in 923. He wrote a vast history of the world and an equally vast commentary on the Qur'an, usually called Jami' al-bayan, the comprehensive explanation. Muslim scholars across the centuries have treated it as the foundation of the whole discipline, the book later commentators quarried.

His method has two steps. For each verse or phrase, he first gathers the reports: what Ibn Abbas said, what Mujahid said, what Qatada said, each with its chain of transmitters. Where the reports agree, he says so. Where they differ, he lays out the options as numbered opinions. Then he takes the second step. He states which reading he judges best and gives his reasons, drawing on Arabic usage, the context of the surah, and the weight of the reports.

That second step matters. Al-Tabari is often called the master of transmitted tafsir, but he does not just repeat. He calls his own selections *ikhtiyar*, a reasoned choice, and he is willing to reject a report from a Companion if the Arabic will not bear it. Historians of the tradition point out that his book is a work of judgment as much as a work of collection. It also preserves hundreds of early opinions that would otherwise be lost.

Consider the Light Verse from the chapter story. Al-Tabari records reports that God is the guide of the people of the heavens and the earth, and reports that the lamp stands for faith in a believer's heart or for the Qur'an itself. He then prefers the reading that God illuminates the heavens and the earth by guiding their inhabitants. A reader can disagree with him, but the reader can see exactly what the choices were. That transparency is why his book is still read.

words.d: Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari (c. 839–923), historian and commentator whose Jami' al-bayan became the model for report-based tafsir
the comprehensive explanation: the title of al-Tabari's commentary on the Qur'an
reasoned choice: a commentator's stated preference among competing readings
the list of people who passed a report from one to the next, used to judge how reliable it is

look.title: When the Commentators Died
look.cite: Standard reference dates; some sources differ by a year
look.prompt: How many centuries separate al-Tabari from Ibn Kathir? Which commentators lived close enough in time to have read one another's work?

check.q: What is the first step of al-Tabari's method for each verse?
choices: He translates the verse into Persian
He asks what philosophy says about the topic
He gathers the transmitted reports with their chains
He explains the verse by a Sufi inner meaning
check.why: Al-Tabari first collects reports from Companions and early scholars, chain by chain, before stating his own preference.

check.q: What does al-Tabari call his own preferred reading among the reports?
choices: Naskh
Ikhtiyar
Tajwid
Isra'iliyyat
check.why: Ikhtiyar means reasoned choice; al-Tabari weighs the reports and states which he judges best. Naskh is abrogation and tajwid is recitation.

check.q: Why do historians say al-Tabari's commentary is more than a collection?
choices: He invented most of the reports himself
He wrote it in verse
He refused to name his sources
He judges the reports and rejects some on grounds of Arabic usage
check.why: Al-Tabari weighs reports against Arabic usage and context, and is willing to reject even a Companion's report, so the book is a work of judgment as well as collection.

lessons.title: Al-Zamakhshari and the Grammar of Meaning
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Zamakhshari's Kashshaf reads the Qur'an through grammar and rhetoric, and through the rationalist theology of the Mu'tazila, which later readers admired and disputed.
reading: Mahmud ibn Umar al-Zamakhshari was born in 1075 in Khwarazm, in Central Asia, and died there in 1144. He was a master of Arabic grammar and rhetoric, and he wrote his commentary, al-Kashshaf, the unveiler, during a stay in Mecca. Where al-Tabari asks who said what, al-Zamakhshari asks how the language works. Why this word and not a near synonym? Why is this clause placed first? What does the verse's rhythm add to its sense?

This approach made the Kashshaf the standard reference for the Qur'an's *i'jaz*, its inimitable eloquence, which Muslims hold to be a sign that the text is from God. Al-Zamakhshari showed, phrase by phrase, how the Qur'an's style does its work. Later commentators of every school borrowed his observations. Even scholars who disliked his theology copied his grammar.

His theology was the problem for many. Al-Zamakhshari belonged to the *Mu'tazila*, a school that held that human reason can know God's justice, that people have real free will, and that God has no body and cannot be seen. He read the Qur'an in that light. Where Surah al-Qiyama (75), ayahs 22–23, describes faces on the Last Day that are radiant, looking toward their Lord, he took the phrase to mean expecting their Lord's reward, since in his view God cannot be seen. Sunni readers of the Ash'ari school, who held that believers will see God, rejected that reading.

The result was a book that everyone used and many warned against. Copies of the Kashshaf circulated with marginal notes correcting its Mu'tazili points, and one later scholar produced an edited version that kept the rhetoric and cut the theology. The Kashshaf shows a pattern that repeats across the tradition: a commentator's theology shapes what a verse is allowed to mean, and rival schools read the same words in opposite ways.

words.d: Mahmud al-Zamakhshari (1075–1144), grammarian of Khwarazm whose Kashshaf is the classic rhetorical commentary
the inimitability of the Qur'an: the Muslim doctrine that its eloquence cannot be matched and is a sign of its divine source
a school of Islamic theology that stressed reason, God's justice, human free will and the view that God cannot be seen
a Sunni school of theology that opposed the Mu'tazila and held, among other things, that believers will see God

look.title: Looking or Waiting?
look.text: Surah al-Qiyama (75), ayahs 22–23, describes faces on that Day that are bright, gazing toward their Lord, in Pickthall's rendering. The Arabic preposition can mean toward, and it is also used in a phrase meaning to await something. Al-Zamakhshari, a Mu'tazili, read the verse as faces awaiting their Lord's reward. Ash'ari commentators read it as faces literally seeing God. Both readings cite the same grammar books.
look.prompt: Explain how a scholar's prior belief about whether God can be seen leads each side to its reading. Is either side changing the words, or only choosing among meanings the words allow?

check.q: What is the main focus of al-Zamakhshari's Kashshaf?
choices: Grammar, rhetoric and the Qur'an's eloquence
The chains of transmitters behind each report
The history of the caliphs
The inner meanings known to Sufi masters
check.why: The Kashshaf is the classic rhetorical commentary, prized for showing the i'jaz, the inimitable eloquence, of the text.

check.q: Which theological school did al-Zamakhshari belong to?
choices: The Ash'ari school
The Twelver Shia
The Mu'tazila
The Hanbali school
check.why: Al-Zamakhshari was a Mu'tazili, and his rationalist theology shaped readings such as his treatment of seeing God in 75:22–23.

check.q: Why did later Sunni scholars both use and warn against the Kashshaf?
choices: It was written in Persian, which few could read
Its grammar was excellent but its theology was Mu'tazili
It contained no explanation of any verse
It was banned by the caliph in Baghdad
check.why: Scholars borrowed the Kashshaf's rhetorical insight while adding notes or edited versions to correct its Mu'tazili positions.

lessons.title: Al-Razi Asks Every Question
lessons.mainIdea: Fakhr al-Din al-Razi turned tafsir into a place for philosophy and theology, listing objections and answers on each verse in his Mafatih al-ghayb.
reading: Fakhr al-Din al-Razi was born in 1149 in Rayy, near modern Tehran, and died in Herat in 1210. He was trained in theology, philosophy, law and the natural sciences, and he taught and debated across Iran and Central Asia. His commentary, Mafatih al-ghayb, the keys of the unseen, is also called simply the Great Commentary. It is one of the longest ever written, and it was left unfinished at his death; students completed it.

Al-Razi's method is the method of the debating hall. On a verse, he states a question. He lists the possible answers, often five or ten. He gives arguments for and against each. Then he decides. The questions range widely. On verses about the sky, he discusses astronomy. On verses about creation, he discusses the philosophers' arguments about whether the world has a beginning. On the opening surah, he wrote at length about the meaning of praise and of God's names.

A famous quip, attributed to later scholars, said that al-Razi's book contained everything except tafsir. The joke has a point and a limit. His pages do wander far from the wording of the verse. But al-Razi thought the wandering was the point. For him the Qur'an invites reflection on nature and on reason, and a commentary should follow the invitation. Surah al-Baqara (2), ayah 164, lists the heavens, the earth, the alternation of night and day, ships, rain and winds as signs for people who use their reason. Al-Razi read verses like this as a mandate for science.

In theology al-Razi was an Ash'ari, and he defended that school against the Mu'tazila and the philosophers. Yet he took the philosophers seriously enough to state their views fairly before answering them, which made his book a reference even for readers who disagreed with him. Historians of Islamic thought describe him as the figure who brought philosophy fully inside the commentary tradition, where it stayed.

words.d: theologian and commentator (1149–1210) whose Mafatih al-ghayb brought philosophy and natural science into tafsir
the keys of the unseen: al-Razi's commentary, also called the Great Commentary
ayat: the Qur'an's word for its verses and also for the wonders of nature it points to as evidence of God

look.title: Signs for Those Who Reason
look.text: Surah al-Baqara (2), ayah 164, says that in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, the ships that sail the sea with what benefits people, the rain God sends down to revive the dead earth, the animals scattered on it, the shifting winds and the clouds held between sky and earth, there are signs for people who use their reason.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:164, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Al-Razi took verses like this as an invitation to discuss astronomy and physics inside a commentary. What in the wording supports that reading? What might a report-based commentator say instead?

check.q: How does al-Razi typically handle a verse in Mafatih al-ghayb?
choices: He quotes the verse and moves on without comment
He gives only the report of Ibn Abbas
He states a question, lists possible answers, argues each and decides
He rewrites the verse in Persian poetry
check.why: Al-Razi's method comes from the debating hall: questions, multiple answers, arguments for and against, and a decision.

check.q: Which school of theology did al-Razi defend?
choices: The Mu'tazila
The Ash'ari school
The Ismaili Shia
The Kharijites
check.why: Al-Razi was an Ash'ari who argued against the Mu'tazila and the philosophers, while stating their views before answering.

check.q: What did the quip that al-Razi's book had everything except tafsir mean?
choices: The book was never finished
The book was lost
The book contained only hadith
The book ranged far into philosophy and science beyond the verse's wording
check.why: The joke pointed to how far al-Razi wandered from the words of each verse into philosophy, theology and natural science.

lessons.title: Ibn Kathir and the Return to Reports
lessons.mainIdea: Ibn Kathir explained the Qur'an first by the Qur'an, then by hadith, then by the Companions, and his method became the most widely printed tafsir of modern times.
reading: Ismail ibn Umar ibn Kathir was born around 1300 near Bosra in Syria and died in Damascus in 1373. He was a historian and a hadith scholar, and a student of Ibn Taymiyya, the Damascus jurist who argued that Muslims should return to the practice of the first generations. Ibn Kathir's commentary, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-azim, put that program to work on the text.

His introduction lays out a ladder. The best tafsir explains the Qur'an by the Qur'an, since what one verse states briefly another explains at length. If that fails, turn to the *Sunna*, the Prophet's example as recorded in hadith. If that fails, turn to the Companions, who saw the revelation come down. Only then, and with caution, turn to the next generation. Opinion for its own sake is not on the ladder. Ibn Kathir also warned against the isra'iliyyat, though he still quoted some.

Take the Throne Verse, Surah al-Baqara (2), ayah 255, which begins, in Pickthall's translation, Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Ibn Kathir explains its phrases by other verses about God's knowledge and power, then cites a hadith in which Muhammad tells the Companion Ubayy ibn Ka'b that this is the greatest verse in the Book of God. He adds reports about reciting it for protection. The verse, the hadith and the Companions' practice are stacked one on the other.

Ibn Kathir's book was respected in its own age, but its fame grew in the twentieth century. Because it is shorter than al-Tabari's, clearer in structure, and cautious about theology and stories, it became the tafsir most often printed, abridged and translated, including into English. Scholars note that this modern popularity says as much about the readers who chose it, and their preference for hadith-based method, as about the medieval book itself.

words.d: Ismail ibn Kathir (c. 1300–1373), Damascus historian and hadith scholar whose tafsir is now the most widely printed
the Prophet's example, as recorded in hadith; the second step on Ibn Kathir's ladder of interpretation
Damascus jurist (1263–1328) who urged a return to the first generations and taught Ibn Kathir
Surah al-Baqara 2:255, called Ayat al-Kursi, which a hadith names the greatest verse in the Qur'an

look.title: The Throne Verse Opens
look.text: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:255, Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Ibn Kathir explains this opening by other verses, then by a hadith calling it the greatest verse. Describe how his ladder of sources shows in that order, and what a Sufi commentator might add instead.

check.q: What is the first step on Ibn Kathir's ladder of interpretation?
choices: Explaining the Qur'an by the Qur'an itself
Consulting the philosophers
Asking the ruler of Damascus
Reading the isra'iliyyat
check.why: Ibn Kathir's introduction says the best tafsir explains the Qur'an by the Qur'an, then by the Sunna, then by the Companions.

check.q: Which teacher shaped Ibn Kathir's program of returning to the first generations?
choices: Al-Zamakhshari
Al-Ghazali
Ibn Taymiyya
Al-Tabari
check.why: Ibn Kathir studied with Ibn Taymiyya in Damascus; al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari died centuries before.

check.q: Why did Ibn Kathir's commentary become the most printed tafsir in modern times?
choices: It was the only one to survive
It is shorter, clearly structured and hadith-based, which suited modern readers' preferences
It was written in English
The Ottoman sultan required it in every mosque
check.why: Scholars note its modern popularity reflects readers' preference for a concise, hadith-based method; al-Tabari's and al-Razi's works also survive.

lessons.title: Shia Commentary and the Imams
lessons.mainIdea: Shia tafsir shares most tools with Sunni tafsir but gives a special place to the Imams as interpreters, as al-Tabrisi's Majma' al-bayan shows.
reading: *Shia* Muslims hold that leadership of the community after Muhammad belonged to Ali, his cousin and son-in-law, and to a line of descendants known as the *Imams*. For Twelver Shia, the largest Shia group, there were twelve. This belief shapes tafsir. Shia scholars hold that the Imams inherited the Prophet's knowledge of the Qur'an's meaning, so reports from the Imams carry a weight in Shia commentary that reports from Companions carry in Sunni commentary.

The most widely used classical Shia commentary is Majma' al-bayan, the gathering of explanation, by al-Fadl ibn al-Hasan al-Tabrisi, who died in 1153 or 1154 in Iran. Historians describe it as remarkably balanced. Al-Tabrisi organizes each passage under headings: the variant readings, the grammar, the occasion of revelation, the meaning. He quotes Sunni authorities freely, including al-Tabari, and then adds the readings passed down from the Imams. Sunni scholars have long cited it in turn.

Where the two traditions differ most is on verses they read as referring to Ali and the Prophet's household. Surah al-Ahzab (33), ayah 33, speaks of God's wish to remove impurity from the people of the house, the ahl al-bayt. Shia commentators, citing reports from the Imams, read the people of the house as Ali, Fatima, Hasan and Husayn, and see the verse as a statement of their purity and authority. Many Sunni commentators, citing the surrounding verses addressed to the Prophet's wives, include the wives in the phrase. Both sides cite hadith; they weigh them differently.

Some early Shia writers also held that the Qur'an as collected had been altered to remove references to Ali. Al-Tabrisi rejected that view firmly, and mainstream Twelver scholarship since has affirmed that the standard text is complete. Historians note the point because it shows that Shia and Sunni commentators, whatever their disputes over meaning, came to share the same text and most of the same tools.

words.d: Muslims who hold that leadership after Muhammad belonged to Ali and his descendants; about one in ten Muslims today
in Shia belief, the divinely guided leaders descended from Ali, whom Shia scholars treat as authoritative interpreters of the Qur'an
Twelver Shia scholar (d. 1153 or 1154) whose Majma' al-bayan is the most used classical Shia commentary
the people of the house: the Prophet's household, a phrase in 33:33 that Shia and Sunni commentators define differently

look.title: Who Are the People of the House?
look.text: Surah al-Ahzab (33), ayah 33, says that God wishes to remove uncleanness from the people of the house and to purify them. The verses just before it address the wives of the Prophet. Shia commentators, citing reports from the Imams and a hadith about the Prophet gathering Ali, Fatima, Hasan and Husayn under his cloak, read the phrase as those five. Many Sunni commentators read it as including the wives, because of the context, while also reporting the cloak hadith.
look.prompt: Each side uses a tool from the toolbox: one leans on context, the other on a report. Explain how the same verse can carry two readings without either side changing a word.

check.q: In Shia tafsir, whose reports carry a weight like that of the Companions in Sunni tafsir?
choices: The Umayyad caliphs
The Imams descended from Ali
The Mu'tazili theologians
The Sufi masters
check.why: Shia scholars hold that the Imams inherited the Prophet's knowledge of the text, so their reports are central to Shia commentary.

check.q: What is Majma' al-bayan?
choices: Al-Tabari's commentary
A Sufi manual on inner meanings
A handbook of the sciences of the Qur'an by al-Suyuti
Al-Tabrisi's Twelver Shia commentary, known for quoting Sunni authorities as well
check.why: Majma' al-bayan is al-Tabrisi's commentary, praised by historians for its balance and for citing al-Tabari and other Sunni scholars.

check.q: How do many Sunni and Shia commentators differ on 33:33?
choices: Sunni scholars deny the verse exists; Shia accept it
Shia read the people of the house as Ali, Fatima, Hasan and Husayn; many Sunni readers include the Prophet's wives
Shia say the verse is about Mecca; Sunni say Medina
Shia scholars read it in Persian; Sunni scholars in Arabic
check.why: The dispute is about who the ahl al-bayt are: Shia readers cite the cloak hadith, and many Sunni readers cite the context addressed to the wives.

lessons.title: Sufi Readings and Inner Meaning
lessons.mainIdea: Sufi commentators such as al-Qushayri read the Qur'an for an inner meaning alongside the outer one, and later thinkers like Ibn Arabi built whole systems on that reading.
reading: *Sufism* is the name for Islam's traditions of inward devotion: remembrance of God, discipline of the self, love and closeness. Sufi commentators did not reject the plain meaning of the Qur'an. They held that beneath the outer sense, the *zahir*, lay an inner sense, the *batin*, that spoke to the soul's journey. A verse about Musa (Moses) crossing the sea could also be read as the soul crossing from fear to trust. Sufis pointed to Surah Qaf (50), ayah 16, which says God is nearer to a person than the jugular vein, as a charter for this closeness.

Abu'l-Qasim al-Qushayri of Nishapur, who died in 1072, wrote a commentary called Lata'if al-isharat, the subtleties of the allusions. The title tells the method. Each verse contains an allusion, an ishara, that the trained heart can catch. Al-Qushayri was also a jurist and a theologian, and he was careful to say the inner reading adds to the outer and never cancels it. Many Sufi commentators quoted a hadith that every verse has an outer and an inner meaning, though scholars of hadith rated it weakly.

Muhyi al-Din Ibn Arabi, born in Murcia in Spain in 1165 and buried in Damascus in 1240, went further. In works like the Fusus al-hikam, the bezels of wisdom, he read the prophets of the Qur'an as facets of a single divine wisdom, and he treated the whole world as a book of signs mirroring the Qur'an. His readers called him the greatest master. His critics, including Ibn Taymiyya, said he had dissolved the line between God and creation. A long commentary printed under his name is now known by scholars to be the work of a later follower, Abd al-Razzaq al-Kashani (d. c. 1330).

Sunni jurists set limits on Sufi reading. An inner meaning was acceptable, most held, if it did not contradict the outer meaning, the Arabic or the law, and if the reader did not claim that his reading was the only one. Within those limits Sufi tafsir flourished for centuries and shaped poetry from Rumi in Persian to Yunus Emre in Turkish. The tradition shows a fourth way of asking what a verse means: not who reported it, how it is phrased, or what reason says, but what it does to the one who reads it.

words.d: Islam's traditions of inward devotion, self-discipline and closeness to God; a Sufi is a follower of these paths
the outer, plain meaning of a verse
the inner meaning of a verse, which Sufi readers held lies beneath the outer one
Sufi scholar of Nishapur (d. 1072) whose Lata'if al-isharat reads each verse for its allusion to the soul's path
Andalusian Sufi thinker (1165–1240) whose readings of the Qur'an built a vast system of divine unity; admired and disputed

look.title: Nearer Than the Jugular Vein
look.text: Surah Qaf (50), ayah 16, says that God created the human being and knows what his soul whispers to him, and that God is nearer to him than his jugular vein.
look.cite: Qur'an 50:16, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: A jurist might read this verse as a statement about God's knowledge. A Sufi might read it as a statement about intimacy. Show how each reading stays with the words, and what each reader is looking for.

check.q: What do zahir and batin mean in Sufi commentary?
choices: The Meccan and Medinan surahs
The outer meaning and the inner meaning of a verse
The Arabic text and its Persian translation
The clear and the abrogated verses
check.why: Zahir is the outer, plain sense and batin the inner sense that Sufi readers sought beneath it, without cancelling the outer.

check.q: What is Lata'if al-isharat?
choices: Al-Qushayri's Sufi commentary on the allusions in each verse
Ibn Kathir's introduction to tafsir
A Shia collection of reports from the Imams
Al-Wahidi's book of occasions of revelation
check.why: Lata'if al-isharat, the subtleties of the allusions, is al-Qushayri's commentary; al-Wahidi wrote on asbab al-nuzul.

check.q: What do scholars now say about the long commentary printed under Ibn Arabi's name?
choices: It was written by al-Tabari
It was never printed
It is the work of his later follower al-Kashani
It is a translation from Latin
check.why: The commentary attributed to Ibn Arabi is generally recognized as the work of Abd al-Razzaq al-Kashani (d. c. 1330).

lessons.title: One Verse in Four Commentaries
lessons.mainIdea: Reading the Light Verse through al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and a Sufi reader shows that method, not the text alone, decides what a commentary says.
reading: Return now to the Light Verse, Surah al-Nur (24), ayah 35. In Pickthall's rendering, God is the light of the heavens and the earth; the likeness of that light is a niche holding a lamp, the lamp in a glass, the glass like a shining star, lit from a blessed olive tree neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow without fire being touched to it; light upon light; God guides to that light whom God wills; and God speaks to people in parables. The verse ends by saying God knows all things. Four kinds of commentator, four kinds of reading.

Al-Tabari lists the reports. Some say the niche is the believer's chest and the lamp is the Qur'an in the believer's heart. Some say the lamp is faith. Some read the whole figure as the light of Muhammad. He prefers the reading that God, as light, guides the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. Al-Zamakhshari, the rhetorician, explains each image as part of a single extended simile and asks why the tree is neither eastern nor western. His answer is that such an olive gets sun all day and gives the purest oil, so the image is about the highest clarity.

Al-Razi asks what light is. He argues that light in the literal sense is a quality of bodies, so God cannot be light literally; the verse must mean that God is the source of all illumination and guidance. He discusses the physics of oil, flame and glass, and he lists opinions on whether the parable describes the Qur'an, the Prophet or the believer. A Sufi reader takes another path. Al-Ghazali (d. 1111), who was both a jurist and a Sufi, devoted a whole treatise to this verse, the Niche of Lights, in which the lamp, glass and tree map the levels of the human spirit rising toward God.

None of the four denies the others' readings. Al-Tabari records inner readings among his reports. Al-Razi cites the philosophers and the Sufis. Al-Ghazali quotes the grammarians. The tradition gave scholars permission to disagree, within limits, because it held that the text has depth. Historians of tafsir put it this way: the classical commentary is not a single answer but a recorded conversation, and each new commentator joined it by quoting the ones before.

words.d: Surah al-Nur 24:35, which compares God's light to a lamp in a niche; a favorite verse of commentators of every school
a short comparison or image that teaches a truth; the Qur'an calls its own such images mathal
jurist, theologian and Sufi (d. 1111) whose Niche of Lights reads 24:35 as a map of the human spirit

look.title: Four First Sentences
look.text: On the Light Verse: Reader A begins, The people of interpretation disagree about the meaning of this, and lists names. Reader B begins by asking whether the sentence is a metaphor and what kind. Reader C begins, Know that light, in the language of the philosophers, is a quality that bodies possess. Reader D begins with the levels of light within the human spirit. These are described from the approaches, not quoted.
look.prompt: Match each reader to al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Ghazali, and say which tool from the commentator's toolbox each reaches for first.

check.q: Which reading of the Light Verse did al-Tabari prefer?
choices: The lamp is the physics of oil and flame
God is the light in a literal sense
The tree is a map of the human spirit
God, as light, guides the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth
check.why: After listing the reports, al-Tabari preferred the reading that God illuminates the heavens and the earth by guiding their people.

check.q: Who wrote the Niche of Lights, a treatise on 24:35?
choices: Al-Ghazali
Al-Tabrisi
Ibn Kathir
Al-Wahidi
check.why: Al-Ghazali (d. 1111) wrote Mishkat al-anwar, the Niche of Lights, reading the verse's images as levels of the spirit.

check.q: What do historians of tafsir mean by calling the classical commentary a recorded conversation?
choices: The commentaries were spoken, never written
Each commentator quoted earlier ones and added his own reading within shared limits
The commentators met in Baghdad to agree on one answer
Only one commentary was allowed per century
check.why: Commentators joined the tradition by citing earlier work and disagreeing within limits; the result is a conversation, not a single verdict.

review.q: Which commentator is known for gathering transmitted reports with their chains and then stating a reasoned choice?
choices: Al-Tabari
Al-Razi
Ibn Arabi
Al-Qushayri
review.why: Al-Tabari's Jami' al-bayan collects reports and then gives his ikhtiyar, his reasoned preference.

review.q: What is the difference between muhkam and mutashabih verses according to 3:7?
choices: Meccan versus Medinan
Long versus short surahs
Clear and decisive versus ambiguous
Recited versus written
review.why: Surah Al Imran 3:7 distinguishes clear verses from ambiguous ones; scholars read the ambiguous in light of the clear.

review.q: Which commentary is prized for rhetoric but was criticized for its Mu'tazili theology?
choices: Tafsir al-Qur'an al-azim by Ibn Kathir
Al-Kashshaf by al-Zamakhshari
Majma' al-bayan by al-Tabrisi
Lata'if al-isharat by al-Qushayri
review.why: Al-Zamakhshari's Kashshaf is the classic rhetorical commentary; its Mu'tazili readings drew corrections from Sunni scholars.

review.q: In Twelver Shia tafsir, what gives the Imams' reports their authority?
choices: The Imams were elected by the community
The Imams wrote the earliest Arabic grammar
The Imams lived in Baghdad
Shia belief that the Imams inherited the Prophet's knowledge of the text
review.why: Shia scholars hold that the Imams, descended from Ali, inherited the Prophet's understanding, so their reports are central to Shia commentary.

choices: The inner meaning of a verse
The occasion on which a verse was revealed
Abrogation: a later verse replacing an earlier ruling
The name of al-Razi's commentary
review.why: Naskh is abrogation; the occasion of revelation is sabab al-nuzul and the inner meaning is batin.

review.q: Which commentator brought philosophy and natural science fully into tafsir, in a book jokingly said to contain everything except tafsir?
choices: Ibn Kathir
Fakhr al-Din al-Razi
Al-Tabari
Muqatil ibn Sulayman
review.why: Al-Razi's Mafatih al-ghayb ranges through astronomy, physics and theology on each verse, which prompted the quip.

review.q: What is the first step on Ibn Kathir's ladder for explaining a verse?
choices: The Qur'an explained by the Qur'an
The reports of the Imams
The philosophers' arguments
The inner meaning known to Sufis
review.why: Ibn Kathir's introduction says the best tafsir explains the Qur'an by the Qur'an, then by the Sunna, then by the Companions.

review.q: What did mainstream Sunni jurists require of a Sufi inner reading?
choices: That it be written in Persian
That it replace the outer meaning
That it come only from Ibn Arabi
That it not contradict the outer meaning, the Arabic or the law
review.why: Most jurists accepted batin readings that added to, but did not cancel, the zahir and did not claim to be the only reading.
